newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Glitches mar foreign investment in Philippines.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Glitches mar foreign investment in Philippines.

text.p: Four years after launching far-reaching reforms which have brought a remarkable turnaround in its economic fortunes, the Philippines is seeking to attract even more foreign investors.
Gross national product growth in the Philippines is set to be a healthy 7.1 percent in 1996 and forecast to rise this year, while inflation is pegged to be contained within 6-7 percent.
Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson said this month that even these optimistic figures are beginning to look conservative.

Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo has said the increase in foreign investment to $1.6 billion in the first half of 1996 from $577 million in the same 1995 period is likely to improve this year as more reforms are put in place and laws are formulated to promote the Philippines as an alternative to Hong Kong as the territory reverts to China.
A rosy picture? Not entirely, say some, pointing to a series of glitches in some of the most high-profile projects in the country involving foreign money.

Among the projects under a cloud are the privatisation of a container terminal at Subic Bay, the sale of the historic Manila Hotel, a project to develop reclaimed land in Manila Bay, bidding out the Manila waterworks and the construction of what will perhaps ultimately be the country's biggest power plant.
SOUR GRAPES?
Some critics have said the glitches are not coincidental and reflect a deeper malaise in the way business is conducted in the Philippines.

Some months ago, the British Ambassador Adrian Thorpe spoke unusually critically and publicly of the string of reverses in contracts. "Even after winning bidders sign contracts, the privatisation process is not exactly a settled matter," he said.
"Foreign companies quite rightly see the Philippines as a good investment opportunity. But there have been a lot of high-publicised cases recently where contracts have not been enforced."

Others say losing bidders in tendered contracts often seek recourse in law courts or petition Congress to reverse decisions. While these acts stem mainly from sour grapes, they have been known to succeed occasionally and otherwise have the effect of long postponements.
THE SUBIC CONTAINER IMBROGLIO

Last year, the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA) decided to offer a 25-year contract to set up a container terminal in the booming economic zone which has replaced the former U.S. military base.

The multi-million dollar contract was awarded to Hong Kong's Hutchison Port Holdings, a unit of Hutchison Whampoa. A losing bidder, local firm International Container Terminal Services protested, and the bidding was re-evaluated.
SBMA again chose Hutchison, but was overruled by President Fidel Ramos. Earlier this month, Ramos ordered SBMA to re-start the bidding process from scratch.
John Meredith, group managing director at Hutchison Ports, said his company will not invest in the Philippines at all if it loses out on the Subic bid.

"I think President Ramos personally is very keen to resolve the issues and get outside investment into the country, but there are others who feel that shouldn't be the case or are protective of local interests," he told Reuters. "Until this is resolved, I think this is going to keep occurring."

Meredith said re-bidding was not possible since all quotations made by his company were now public knowledge. "There comes a time when you have to say enough is enough," he said, adding that Hutchison was seeking legal advice on whether Ramos had the power to overrule the autonomous SBMA.

-- In January last year, the Supreme Court put on hold the 1995 auction of the historic Manila Hotel to the Malaysian firm Renong Bhd after a losing local bidder said Filipinos should be given priority in the acquisition of state assets. No final decision has been made.
-- In May, the government cancelled a 3.1 billion peso radar contract awarded to GEC-Marconi after a senator complained that the deal was overpriced.

-- A contract to build the country's largest power project, a 1,200 megawatt gas- fired plant, was re-bid last year after the government said the winning offer from Hong Kong's Consolidated Electric Power Asia, then a unit of Hopewell Holdings, was based on banned technology. The final award has not been made, but the government has said the Korea Electric Power Corp has posted the lowest bid at $1.457 billion.

-- Ramos has ordered a review of contracts involving the development of some 1,500 hectares (3,707 acres) of land reclaimed from Manila Bay. Senators have said at least one of the seven contracts, awarded to a Thai-Filipino consortium, is grossly undervalued although the companies concerned have denied any wrong-doing.

-- Bidding for the world's largest water privatisation programme, two 25-year contracts worth an estimated $7 billion to supply water to Metro Manila, got underway this month. A suit filed by a local company which fears that the privatisation could affect its chances to develop a water source was due to be heard on January 20, three days before the bids are announced. Among the companies bidding are the Bechtel Corp of the United States, United Utilities Plc, Lyonnaise des Eaux SA, Anglian Water Plc, Australia Water Technologies Pty Ltd and Compagnie Generale de Eaux.
ANALYSTS STILL SEE ROSY PICTURE
Despite the problems, the Philippines is still an attractive destination for foreign investments, analysts in the region say.

"Fundamentally, the economy is extremely attractive for foreign investment. As the economy begins to establish itself on a higher growth trajectory, there are growing opportunities for investment," said Desmond Supple, an economist with the Singapore-based IDEA consultancy.
He said the problems, like the row over the Subic container terminal, "could lead to some slippage in foreign investment inflows".
"But given the economic attractiveness of the Philippines, despite this blow-up, I would still expect investment to be strong," he said.

Former foreign secretary Roberto Romulo, now the chairman of the Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co, said the free-wheeling democracy in the country, one of the biggest attractions to foreign investors, was one reason for the glitches.
"In any democratic country, there will be litigation," he said. "Some of it will be warranted, some of it will be unwarranted."
But he added that the Philippines was in a far better position to attract foreign investment than in years past.

"In 1992, when I was foreign secretary, I had the most difficult job selling the Philippines," Romulo said. "It was like selling the sizzle on the steak when there was no steak. Today, I would suggest that there is a great deal of substance and meat."
